analysis.one_liner: Sends middle-income households a wartime cost-of-living tax credit and bans price gouging on fuel and staples.
analysis.headline: Introduced in April 2026 and referred to two committees, the bill has sat without action and attracted no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a temporary, refundable tax credit for households earning between $80,000 and $160,000 to offset increases in commuting, grocery, and utility costs tied to the war involving the United States, Israel, and Iran. It would also make it an unfair trade practice to charge 'grossly excessive' prices for motor fuel, home heating fuels, electricity, and essential consumer staples during the emergency, enforceable by the Federal Trade Commission and the Justice Department. Everything in the bill would end when the war-related energy emergency does.
analysis.who_benefits: Middle-income households between $80,000 and $160,000 of income would receive a refundable tax credit sized to their family and region to offset war-driven increases in gas, grocery, and utility bills. Consumers generally would gain a federal backstop against extreme price spikes on fuel and basic necessities during the emergency, in addition to existing state price-gouging laws.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a refundable tax credit for middle-income households ($80,000-$160,000), sized by the Treasury Secretary to offset average increases in commuting, grocery, and utility costs caused by the conflict, adjusted for family size and regional costs.

Makes it an unfair or deceptive act to sell motor fuel, home heating fuels, electricity, or essential consumer staples at a grossly excessive increase over pre-enactment prices that is not explained by actual cost increases.

Gives both the Federal Trade Commission and the Justice Department authority to enforce the anti-gouging ban, seek civil penalties and restitution for consumers, and preserves state price-gouging laws and state attorney general enforcement.
Directs the FTC to study how state and local price-gouging laws worked during the war-related disruptions and recommend whether a permanent federal standard is warranted.

analysis.who_pays: Fuel wholesalers and retailers, utilities, and grocery and household-staples sellers would bear the risk of penalties and restitution if their wartime price increases cannot be tied to real cost increases. The Treasury would fund the tax credit out of general revenue, and the FTC and Justice Department would absorb enforcement costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fuel and staples sellers; federal taxpayers

drawbacks.text: A federal price-gouging prohibition on food and fuel can discourage sellers from building up supply or quickly passing through genuine cost increases, and critics argue such caps can worsen shortages during a real supply shock.

The credit amount is left entirely to Treasury Department discretion ('reasonably calculated' to offset average cost increases), so the benefit is not a defined dollar figure and could be set low or administered inconsistently.

Covering 'essential consumer staples, including food and basic household necessities' as defined by the FTC is broad and imprecise, which could invite litigation and uneven enforcement across sellers.

The emergency period and the credit's phase-out depend on presidential ceasefire certification and a joint cabinet certification that prices have normalized, so the program's duration is tied to executive determinations rather than a fixed date.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The relief is real but targeted: it aims a temporary credit at households too well-off for most low-income programs but without large savings, and adds a wartime enforcement backstop on top of state gouging laws. The costs are a new federal cap on pricing in huge markets (fuel, food, electricity) with vaguely defined triggers and a discretionary credit amount, and the whole structure sunsets with the emergency. On paper the consumer benefits are concrete and the main risks are design imprecision; the practical obstacle so far is not the design but the lack of any political support beyond the sponsor.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on April 9, 2026 and sent to the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees, where it has not moved since.

narrative.text: Rep. Cherfilus-McCormick introduced the W.A.R. Act on April 9, 2026, targeting relief at middle-income households facing war-driven energy and grocery costs.
The bill was referred to the Committee on Ways and Means and, in addition, to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, with no further action recorded.
No members have signed on as cosponsors.
The 119th Congress remains in session, so the bill is still alive but has no scheduled committee consideration or floor action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has had to change behavior: fuel and grocery sellers face no new federal price restrictions, and no middle-income household has received any new credit. Whichever side benefits will be determined by whether the bill ever gets committee attention, and with no cosponsors it currently has almost none.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; the bill has simply stalled.

for.name: Rep. Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its middle-income tax credit and anti-price-gouging provisions.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred and no opposition has been recorded; the bill has a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party.

industries.industry: Fuel wholesalers and retailers (gasoline, diesel, heating oil)
industries.note: The bill would expose them to FTC and DOJ penalties and consumer restitution for wartime price increases that exceed their documented cost increases. Their interest in keeping wartime pricing unrestricted runs directly against the consumers paying those prices at the pump and at home.

Home heating fuels and electricity are covered goods, so wartime rate increases would face a federal 'grossly excessive' standard for the first time during this emergency. Households paying war-inflated heating and power bills would sit on the other side of that line.

Food and basic household necessities fall under the price-gouging prohibition, a market where federal anti-gouging enforcement does not currently exist outside state laws. Ordinary shoppers would gain the protection; large staples sellers would gain exposure.

The refundable credit is paid from general revenue, and its size is left to the Treasury Secretary's calculation, so the fiscal cost is open-ended while the emergency lasts. It is targeted to a defined income band, which limits but does not fix the exposure.

analysis.trajectory: A single-sponsored tax and trade-regulation bill sitting in both Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce with zero cosponsors almost never reaches a markup or the floor; the realistic path is that it stays dormant unless the sponsor builds bipartisan support or leadership attaches the concept to larger emergency or tax legislation.
